strengths: ColorCtrl addresses a practically important problem and presents a simple, intuitive decomposition of MM-DiT attention: vision-to-vision attention preserves structure, vision-to-text attention localizes the edit, visual value tokens preserve unedited colors, and text-to-vision attention enables attribute reweighting.

The empirical study is broad, covering SD3, FLUX.1-dev, CogVideoX, real-image inversion, and two instruction-based editing models. Comparisons include numerous training-free methods and commercial systems.

Results consistently show strong preservation metrics across PIE-Bench and the larger 300-pair ColorCtrl-Bench. The qualitative examples also demonstrate compelling edits involving reflections, illumination, multiple objects, and different materials.
Component ablations, mask-threshold analysis, additional gradient-based metrics, failure cases, implementation settings, and ethical considerations improve the paper's transparency.
weaknesses: The strongest physical-consistency claims are not rigorously established. Canny/gradient similarity and background PSNR/SSIM do not demonstrate preservation of geometry, material parameters, illumination intensity, or physically correct light transport; the rendering formulation is descriptive rather than an identified or enforced physical model.

The primary noise-to-image protocol gives ColorCtrl privileged access to paired source/target sampling trajectories, source prompts, attention maps, and value tokens. Commercial systems instead receive a rendered image and instruction, making the claimed superiority to commercial editing models not fully apples-to-apples.

The video experiments do not measure temporal coherence: all quantitative metrics are computed independently per frame, while only three selected frames are shown qualitatively. Thus the claimed advantage in temporal consistency is insufficiently supported.

Every benchmark experiment uses a single seed, with no multi-seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is particularly limiting for stochastic generation and a benchmark containing only 40 PIE-Bench prompt pairs.

The user study is inadequately reported and internally confusing: it is described as pairwise evaluation, yet the method preferences sum to 100%, six baselines receive exactly 0%, and the manuscript does not explain the number of judgments, aggregation procedure, uncertainty calculation, inter-rater agreement, or sampling of the 34 cases.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The paper omits precise details for aggregating masks across heads/layers/timesteps, aligning changed token sequences, choosing attribute-reweighting coefficients, and measuring runtime or memory. Code is only promised after acceptance, and several baselines are author reimplementations with manually tuned settings.

Novelty is moderate: the method primarily combines attention-map replacement, attention-derived masking, value-token copying, and token reweighting, all closely related to prior attention-control approaches. Its value is mainly in the MM-DiT-specific combination and empirical effectiveness rather than a substantial new technical principle.

ColorCtrl-Bench is generated by an LLM without a reported validation process, category statistics, deduplication analysis, or evidence that its prompts are representative rather than favorable to the proposed method. Real-image evaluation is also narrower and uses only two training-free baselines.

ColorCtrl is conceptually simple: it combines vision-to-vision attention transfer for structural preservation, attention-derived masks, and source-value injection outside the edited region. This simplicity could make the method useful in practice.
The evaluation spans SD3, FLUX.1-dev, CogVideoX, and two instruction-based editors, and includes comparisons with several training-free and commercial systems.
The reported preservation improvements are large and generally consistent across Canny-SSIM, background PSNR/SSIM, gradient metrics, qualitative examples, and component ablations.
The paper includes real-image examples, multi-object cases, failure cases, threshold sensitivity, a user study, and an appropriate high-level discussion of misuse and inherited model bias.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation is not representative of ordinary image editing. Source images are generated from the source prompt with the same diffusion model and seed, and the target is generated through a paired branch. This controlled noise-to-image setting substantially favors attention reuse and does not establish equally strong performance on arbitrary user images. Real-image evaluation is much smaller, depends on a separate inversion method, compares against only two baselines, and does not clearly report the number of evaluated examples.

The strongest claims—preservation of geometry, material properties, illumination, reflection/refraction, and physical light-matter interactions—are not directly evaluated. Canny/gradient similarity and background pixel metrics measure appearance preservation, not latent geometry, BRDF/material constancy, light-source parameters, or physical correctness. The rendering formulation therefore overstates what the method or experiments demonstrate.

Edit success and preservation are not cleanly disentangled. Copying source attention and values is naturally rewarded by most reported metrics, while ColorCtrl is below commercial systems on CLIP and, in several settings, semantic-consistency scores. Qualitative arguments that the commercial outputs are merely oversaturated do not replace a rigorous evaluation of whether the requested target color was achieved.

Baseline fairness is difficult to verify. Several methods were reimplemented and assigned method-specific layer/timestep ranges by the authors, while ColorCtrl is evaluated in its preferred all-layer/all-timestep configuration. The manuscript gives neither systematic tuning sweeps nor reproduction of published reference numbers. Comparisons against commercial editors are additionally conducted on images generated by SD3 or FLUX, a distribution especially favorable to ColorCtrl's paired-generation mechanism.

The method relies on the benchmark-provided “blended word” or subject token as an oracle for mask extraction. It is therefore not demonstrated that a user instruction alone suffices, especially for arbitrary real images, ambiguous references, or multiple same-class instances. The source-prompt requirements for real-image use are also insufficiently explained.

ColorCtrl-Bench consists of GPT-generated prompts in essentially the same template as PIE-Bench. There is no independent validation of its diversity, ambiguity, leakage, or difficulty, and all benchmark results use a single random seed. Seed-level robustness, variance, confidence intervals, and statistical significance are missing despite generative results being stochastic.

The user study is inadequately specified. It uses only 34 cases and reports one aggregate preference table without the number and allocation of pairwise judgments, inter-rater agreement, per-baseline sample counts, hypothesis tests, or a clear explanation for every training-free baseline receiving exactly 0% preference. The reported uncertainty is consequently hard to interpret.

The contribution is largely an incremental combination of known attention swapping, attention-mask extraction, and value-token replacement. The paper provides no deeper analysis showing that the claimed semantic roles of the four attention quadrants are causal or general across architectures.

Attribute re-weighting is supported only by selected qualitative examples. Multiplying selected pre-softmax logits does not in general guarantee monotonic strengthening because logits can be negative and softmax is shift-sensitive under such selective scaling. No quantitative controllability, monotonicity, or robustness study is provided.

Reproducibility remains limited because code is promised only after acceptance. Important operational details—attention aggregation across heads/layers/timesteps, mask resizing and token selection, precise re-weighting equations, storage overhead, runtime, and memory—are absent or incomplete. The claim of no additional computational cost also overlooks the source pass and substantial attention/value caching unless these costs are explicitly amortized.

Overall, the paper contains a plausible and potentially useful technique, but the evaluation design and metric choices do not support its broad physical-consistency, robustness, and state-of-the-art claims. These are substantive issues rather than minor omissions, placing it below the acceptance threshold.

The manuscript is clear and visually well supported. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/ccb5f740a5c045c5aa44d8f4caac1834/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical results are consistently strong across SD3 and FLUX.1-dev. On both PIE-Bench and the larger 300-prompt ColorCtrl-Bench, the method substantially improves structural and background-preservation metrics while retaining competitive edit alignment.

The evaluation is broader than is typical for a training-free editing paper: it includes multiple open-source and commercial baselines, image and video generation, real-image inversion, instruction-based editors, component ablations, additional gradient and VLM-based metrics, and a downstream synthetic-data application.

Qualitative examples demonstrate difficult capabilities, including recoloring reflections, illumination, translucent materials, multiple objects, and small localized regions. The reported generalization to CogVideoX, Step1X-Edit, and FLUX.1 Kontext dev strengthens the practical significance.

The method apparently uses one shared configuration across several backbones and all layers and timesteps, avoiding the extensive layer/timestep selection required by competing attention-control approaches.
The paper acknowledges localization and inversion failures, discusses misuse and inherited model bias, and provides substantial implementation detail.
weaknesses: The strongest claim—preservation of geometry, material properties, and physically consistent light-matter interactions—is not directly established. The rendering formulation is conceptual rather than a proved disentanglement, while the evaluation mainly uses 2D edge/background similarity and VLM judgments. Controlled rendered scenes with ground-truth albedo, material, illumination, and geometry would be needed to substantiate physical consistency.

The benchmark evaluation uses only one fixed seed. Because generation and attention localization can be seed-sensitive, results across multiple seeds with uncertainty estimates are important, particularly for the 40-example PIE-Bench subset.

The video evaluation averages image metrics frame by frame and therefore does not directly measure temporal coherence, despite temporal consistency being a central claimed advantage. Temporal perceptual metrics and a video-focused human study are missing.

The user-study reporting is internally unclear. It is described as pairwise evaluation by 24 experts, but Table 7 presents a single distribution over nine methods, with six methods receiving exactly 0%; the percentages are exact multiples of 1/34 rather than reflecting 24×34 judgments. The aggregation procedure, number of judgments per pair, inter-rater agreement, and statistical tests should be clarified.

Several methodological details required for independent reproduction are underspecified, including how attention masks are aggregated across heads, layers, and timesteps; how masks map to value-token grids; handling of multi-token subjects and unequal prompt lengths; and the exact attribute-reweighting transformation. Code is promised only after acceptance.

The comparison depends heavily on author reimplementations and manually tuned intervention ranges for several baselines. A more systematic tuning protocol, validation split, sensitivity analysis, and results using official implementations where possible would make the comparisons more persuasive.

The claimed absence of additional computational cost is misleading: caching avoids recomputing the source branch during the target pass, but producing the cache still requires a full source pass and potentially substantial storage for attention maps and values. Runtime, peak memory, and cache size are not reported.
Attribute reweighting is supported almost entirely by selected qualitative examples. Quantitative monotonicity, controllability, failure rates, and sensitivity to scaling factors are not evaluated.

The core operations build closely on prior attention replacement, attention-derived masking, and value transfer techniques. The particular MM-DiT decomposition is useful, but the conceptual novelty is moderate rather than transformative. Overall, the results make the paper marginally competitive for acceptance, while the evaluation and reproducibility gaps prevent a stronger rating.
